hints: Think about what life was like on Alderney before the 1960s - hedgehogs were completely new there, so what natural checks on their numbers might have been missing?
Now link survival to breeding - what features of a small omnivorous mammal help it produce many surviving offspring when food is plentiful and enemies are few?
walkthrough:
Picture a New Island Home With No Enemies**
When just six hedgehogs arrive on an island where they have never lived, they leave behind many of the things that normally kill them. There are likely few or no predators that recognise them as prey, little competition from similar species, and fewer diseases.

Plenty of Food Means Many Surviving Babies**
Hedgehogs are omnivores, so they can eat insects, worms, fruits and many other foods. With lots of food and few deaths, more young survive to adulthood and they breed quickly with a short generation time, so 6 can become 600 in about 50 years.
Final answer: Few / no predators and little competition on the island; plenty of food available as omnivores with a wide diet and high birth rate / short generation time.

hints: Start with the numbers - only three pairs founded the whole population of 600. What does that tell you about how much genetic variation was present at the start?
Remember blonde spines are coded by a recessive allele. What kind of mating in a tiny isolated population makes a recessive trait show up much more often?
If blonde individuals survive and breed well on this island, what happens over generations to the frequency of that allele?
walkthrough:
A Tiny Starting Gene Pool**
Only six individuals carry all the alleles for the future 600 hedgehogs. That is a classic founder effect. The gene pool is very small with little genetic variation, so by chance the blonde recessive allele may have been common in those founders and its frequency is changed by genetic drift.

Inbreeding Brings Out the Recessive Trait**
On a small island, close relatives must mate with each other. Inbreeding greatly increases the chance of offspring being homozygous recessive. Since blonde needs two copies of the recessive allele, inbreeding makes the 60% blonde phenotype much more likely than in a large mainland population.

Selection Can Then Push It Higher**
If blonde spines give even a small selective advantage on Alderney, for example better camouflage or less predation, those individuals survive and breed more successfully. This is directional selection, which increases the frequency of the blonde allele generation after generation.

Final answer: Small founder population gives small gene pool / founder effect / genetic drift; inbreeding increases homozygosity so recessive blonde allele is expressed more; directional selection as blonde phenotype has selective advantage so allele frequency increases.

hints: Think from the point of view of a native animal or plant that has lived on the island for thousands of years - what happens when a new hungry omnivore suddenly arrives?
Focus on two direct interactions - how could the newcomer take food or living space, and how could it directly harm natives by eating them?
Remember the newcomer also left its own predators and diseases behind - how does that help it breed faster than natives?
Zoom out to the whole ecosystem - what is the long-term result for food webs and biodiversity if natives decline or disappear?
walkthrough:
Competition Takes Food Away From Natives**
An invasive omnivore like the hedgehog eats a wide range of invertebrates, eggs, fruits and more. That means it competes directly with native species for the same food, niche and resources, reducing the food source available for natives.

Predation Directly Kills Natives**
The alien species may also feed on native species themselves, for example ground-nesting bird eggs, snails or insects that have no defence against this new predator. Native prey have not evolved with it, so they are very vulnerable.

Invaders Breed Out of Control**
Alien species often have no natural predators or grazers in the new area and may breed more successfully than natives. Their numbers explode while native numbers fall, and they can also bring new diseases to which natives have no immunity.

Whole Ecosystems Are Damaged**
Together, competition, predation and disease disrupt habitats, food chains and food webs. Populations of natives crash and some may become extinct, so overall biodiversity falls. That is why control is important to protect native communities.

Final answer: Alien species compete with native species for food / niche / resources / light; prey on / feed on native species; breed more successfully and have no natural predators; disrupt habitats / food webs, introduce disease and reduce biodiversity / cause extinction.
